# Iridium Polypyridyl Carboxylates as Excited-State PCET Catalysts for the Functionalization of Unactivated C–H Bonds

**Authors:** Diego A. Granados; Y. Emily Du; Shiloh J. Andersson; Avery Cirincione-Lynch; Kai Cui; Adam Reinhold; Philip D. Jeffrey; Gregory D. Scholes; Sharon Hammes-Schiffer; Robert R. Knowles

**Affiliations:** Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544

## Abstract

The design of catalysts capable of functionalizing unactivated C(sp3)–H bonds remains a significant goal in synthetic organic chemistry. Herein, we present a novel set of iridium polypyridyl complexes bearing pendent Brønsted basic carboxylates that become potent hydrogen atom abstraction catalysts upon visible light irradiation. Thermochemical and spectroscopic characterization reveal that these excited-state complexes exhibit bond dissociation free energies (BDFEs) of up to 105 kcal mol−1 with long excited-state lifetimes. We demonstrate that these complexes can catalyze C–H alkylation reactions in which the Ir carboxylate mediates both C–H abstraction and formation steps. Mechanistic, spectroscopic, and computational studies are consistent with a mechanism for C–H abstraction proceeding through an excited-state proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) mechanism. The modular nature of these Ir polypyridyl complexes establishes a foundation for designing tunable and efficient C–H functionalization catalysts based on covalent tethering of excited-state oxidants and bases.

## Abstract

## Introduction

Proton-coupled electron transfers (PCET) are non-classical redox events in which a proton and electron move together, resulting in the net transfer of a hydrogen atom (Figure 1A).1-4 The importance of concerted PCET is evident from its prevalence in biological redox pathways,5,6 as well as important technologies for energy conversion and storage.7-9 Building from these precedents, oxidative PCET has also been successfully applied as a strategy in organic synthesis, allowing for direct and catalytic radical generation from protic functional groups, such as the E–H bonds of amides,10 sulfonamides,11 and alcohols.12 In these reactions, an oxidant and Brønsted base pair can jointly remove a proton and an electron (often in a concerted process) from the substrate, generating the corresponding heteroatom-centered radical intermediates. While the state of the art in this area has advanced considerably in recent years, analogous PCET methods for the homolytic activation of aliphatic C–H bonds remain much less well developed.13

This can be understood in part by considering the relationship between molecularity and chemoselectivity in PCET processes. A direct termolecular reaction between a base, an oxidant, and a substrate is kinetically unfavorable. Therefore, association of at least two components is critical to PCET reactivity, enabling a more favorable bimolecular transition state (Figure 1B). The mode of association also has profound impacts on the chemoselectivity of the bond activation. The use of chemically independent base and oxidant combinations enforces chemoselectivity for polar protic bonds that can act as hydrogen-bond donors. Substrates containing these bonds can form non-covalent complexes with the Brønsted base prior to reaction with the oxidant, enhancing the reactivity of these bonds (Figure 2A). In contrast, the homolytic activation of aliphatic C–H bonds through decoupled oxidant-base pairs is often precluded by their poor H-bond donor properties, even if PCET is thermodynamically feasible.

The requirement for non-covalent association is removed for PCET systems in which two components are strongly associated. Mayer and coworkers have shown that covalently linked fluorenyl benzoates (substrate-base compounds), wherein the proton acceptor is proximal to the C(sp3)–H bond, react with external oxidants to generate fluorenyl radicals and carboxylic acids by oxidative PCET (Figure 2A).14 Our group has demonstrated similar reactivity by generating arene radical cations to act as internal oxidants alongside weak external bases for the homolytic cleavage of alcohol O–H bonds. Numerous mechanistic studies have also demonstrated that Brønsted basic functionality within the ligand sphere of a redox active metal center can engage in concerted PCET reactivity.15-22 Excited-state PCET reactivity has similarly been reported for metal chromophore complexes bearing both Brønsted bases or acids, including the reaction of Ru polypyridyl complexes with various O–H bonds by Wenger and Paul.19,23-27 Furthermore, the Peters group demonstrated the catalytic reduction of olefins via excited-state reductive C–H PCET, through linked redox-acidobasic components consisting of a ferrocene tethered to an acidic anilinium and a photoresponsive anthracene unit.28

By extension, the covalent association between an oxidant and base also permits the multisite oxidative PCET of C–H bonds without the need for pre-association of the substrate. For example, CYP450 enzymes react with strong aliphatic C–H bonds by an initial bimolecular PCET step involving a covalently-associated basic FeIV oxo and an oxidizing ligand-centered porphyrin radical cation (Figure 2B).29,30 Another example is the oxidative activity of vanadium phosphorus oxide (VPO), a heterogeneous catalyst involved in the industrial synthesis of maleic anhydride from butane gas. Computational studies by Goddard revealed that this reaction proceeds by a PCET-type mechanism, wherein terminal basic phosphates and oxidizing vanadium oxo species can jointly remove a proton and electron from butane.31 A notable small-molecule example was reported by Mayer, in which a well-defined Ru complex featured a terpyridine ligand substituted with a pendent carboxylate.32 This complex (BDFEO–H = 81 kcal mol−1) was shown to react with the weak C–H bond of xanthene to yield bixanthyl product (Figure 2C).

These examples create an interesting prospect for the design of novel PCET catalysts for C–H abstraction, where the association of a proton acceptor and single-electron oxidant can enable concerted PCET reactivity with C–H substrates. In 2019, our group in collaboration with the Alexanian group developed a C–H alkylation protocol that employed a non-covalently associated Ir-phosphate complex that abstracts C–H bonds via pseudo-bimolecular PCET.33 Owing to the enhanced redox potential afforded by visible-light irradiation of the Ir photocatalyst, this catalyst oxidant-base combination was able to efficiently cleave strong C–H bonds (BDFEeff = 103 kcal mol−1).34 However, the excited-state of the Ir-phosphate complex was less emissive and shorter-lived compared that of the unbound Ir catalyst. Moreover, this system was sensitive to competitive hydrogen-bonding to either the photocatalyst or the base. We questioned whether adapting this strategy by covalently associating the proton acceptor to the Ir polypyridyl complex would improve the photophysical properties and catalytic activity. Within this framework, we reasoned that redox potential and pKa could be adjusted by varying the substituents of the individual ligands, providing access to a broad range of BDFE values. Herein, we report the successful realization of these ideas and describe the design, synthesis, characterization, and catalytic applications of two distinct Ir polypyridyl complexes bearing covalently bound carboxylate bases that perform bimolecular excited-state PCET of unactivated C–H bonds with BDFEs up to 105 kcal mol−1 (Figure 3).

## Results and Discussion

With these design principles in mind, we synthesized two complexes, [Ir(dF(CF3)ppy)2(mcbpy–H)]PF6 (mcbpy–H = 4-CO2Me,4’-CO2H-bpy; [IrIII−1H]PF6) and [Ir(d(CF3)(CF3)ppy)2(mcbpy–H)]PF6 ([IrIII−2H]PF6), and their analogous deprotonated congeners IrIII−1 and IrIII−2 for our initial studies (Figure 4A). The zwitterionic complexes IrIII−1 and IrIII−2 were characterized via single crystal X-ray crystallography (Figure 4B). Upon exposure to visible light (420 nm) complex IrIII−1 was found to be emissive, with λ10% = 460 nm (the wavelength at which emission is 10% of the maximum; E0,0 = 62.2 kcal mol−1), while its protonated form [IrIII−1H]PF6 exhibited red shifted emission with λ10% = 500 nm (E0,0 = 57.2 kcal mol−1) (Figure 4C, Figure 5A). The increased triplet energy of IrIII−1 relative to protonated [IrIII−1H]PF6 can be attributed to the greater electron density on the bipyridine ligand following deprotonation, which destabilizes a putative metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) state of the excited state *IrIII−1 (vide infra). Protonation-state dependent emission has previously been observed in analogous MLCT states of Ru polypyridyl carboxylate complexes by Meyer, in which the hypsochromic shift in the deprotonated state was attributed to decreased electron-deficient nature of the deprotonated carboxylate, a signature of photobasic behavior.35,36

We next measured the redox properties of the complex by cyclic voltammetry (Figure 5A). Both IrIII−1 and [IrIII−1H]PF6 featured reversible electrochemical behavior upon reduction (E1/2(III/II) = −1.49 V and −1.28 V, respectively; reported in MeCN vs. Fc+/Fc, Figure S7 and S8). Based on the measured triplet energies and reduction potentials, the excited-state reduction potentials for *IrIII−1 and *[IrIII−1H]PF6 were predicted to be 1.21 V and 1.22 V. Through NMR titration with collidinium triflate,37 the pKa of [IrIII−1H]OTf was determined to be 14.5 in MeCN. These values in turn allowed an estimate of the excited-state pKa (*pKa) of *[IrIII−1H]PF6 to be 17.8 (see SI Section S12 for details). Using these thermochemical values, the ground-state BDFE of IrII−1H was determined to be 43 kcal mol−1. By considering excited-state properties, the BDFE of *IrIII−1 was calculated to be 105 kcal mol−1, indicating that this excited-state complex is a potent H-atom acceptor. The relationships between all ground- and excited-state thermochemical properties are summarized in a “wedge” scheme (Figure 5B). 27

To study the electronic effects of ligand substitution on photocatalyst reactivity, a photocatalyst bearing more electron-deficient phenylpyridine ligands IrIII−2 was synthesized and characterized analogously (Figure 5A). We hypothesized that IrIII−2 would have a higher oxidation potential than IrIII−1 and accordingly, a higher BDFE. In contrast to Ir-1, which was photobasic and featured blue-shifted emission spectra compared to that of [IrIII−1]PF6, the emission spectra of Ir-2 demonstrated a slight redshift compared to that of [IrIII−2]PF6. Similarly to the electron-deficient Ru photocatalysts studied by Meyer, this small bathochromic shift suggested that the LUMO of IrIII−2 is situated on the phenylpyridine ligands (vide infra), rather than the bipyridine ligand. The change in LUMO position renders the excited state of the complex photoacidic. By the same thermochemical analysis, the ground-state O–H BDFE of the IrII−2H state was determined to be 44 kcal mol−1, while the excited species *IrIII−2 possessed a BDFE of 100 kcal mol−1.

From a synthetic perspective, the BDFE values of *IrIII−1 (105 kcal mol−1) and *IrIII−2 (100 kcal mol−1) represent substantial driving forces for C–H abstraction, comparable to strong H-atom abstractors such as cytochrome P450 enzymes29 and polyoxometalates like the excited state of the decatungstate polyanion.13,38 Additionally, the singly-reduced and protonated post-PCET complexes IrII−1H and IrII−2H feature unusually weak O–H bonds (43 kcal mol−1 and 44 kcal mol−1, respectively), suggesting that they may also serve as potent H-atom donors. These thermochemical measurements show that excited-state Ir polypyridyl oxidant-base conjugates are thermodynamically competent to facilitate both hydrogen atom abstraction and donation steps, suggesting that they may be effective as single-component catalysts for PCET-based C–H functionalization (Figure 5C).

### Computational Modeling of Thermochemical Data

To computationally validate key thermodynamic values and gain insight into the excited-state electronic structure of the complexes, we conducted density functional theory (DFT) and time-dependent DFT (TDDFT) studies on IrIII−1, [IrIII−1H], IrIII−2 and [IrIII−2H].39 Various functionals, including long-range corrected functionals, were evaluated (as described in the Supporting Information section S14.1). The B3LYP-D3(BJ) functional40-43 with empirical dispersion provided the most consistent results when compared to experiment and was used for all subsequent calculations. The 6-31G** basis set44,45 was used for all non-metallic atoms, and the LANL2DZ basis set46-48 was used for iridium. The calculations were performed in implicit solvent using the conductor-like polarizable continuum model (C-PCM).49,50 Note that the characters of the natural transition orbitals (NTOs) obtained with TDDFT varied among the functionals tested (see supporting information Section S14.2).

All values were calculated through an isodesmic approach. The computed emission λmax values of the complexes were in good agreement with experimental values (see Table S13). The differences in free energies of the triplet state and the reduced ground state (Figure 5B) were used to compute the corresponding excited-state reduction potentials,51 with the ground state oxidation potential as the reference. The excited-state *pKa of IrIII−1H and IrIII−2H were computed to be 18.3 and 13.3 in MeCN, within one unit of experimental measurements. Although the *BDFE of IrIII−1 and IrIII−2 were experimentally determined through a thermochemical cycle, the computational *BDFE was determined with cyclohexane as a reference for the BDFE.

### Reactivity of Excited-State Ir Carboxylate Complexes with C–H bonds

The thermodynamic values obtained for both IrIII−1 and IrIII−2 suggest that the deprotonated excited state has sufficient driving force to enable PCET activation of bonds as strong as 105 kcal mol−1 (Figure 5C). To evaluate the ability of this excited state to react with C–H bonds, we performed steady-state luminescence quenching experiments with IrIII−1 in the presence of cyclohexane. These experiments measure the rate of deactivation of the excited state of the luminescent photocatalyst in the presence of various quenching species. Steady state luminescence quenching of *IrIII−1 by cyclohexane was observed to follow first-order kinetics, yielding a quenching rate constant (kq) of 1.24 × 106 M−1 s−1 (Figure 6A). Analogous time-resolved quenching experiments via transient absorption spectroscopy (TAS) resulted in a similar quenching constant (kq = 1.97 × 106 M−1 s−1). Furthermore, analogous steady-state experiments with the deuterated cyclohexane (d12-Cy) revealed a lower quenching rate constant of 9.75 × 105 M−1 s−1, corresponding to a KIE (kH/kD) for deactivation of the excited state of 1.3. Notably, small primary KIEs are not uncommon in PCET reactions.52-54 These observations indicate that reaction between the excited state of *IrIII−1 and the alkane substrate is isotopically sensitive, consistent with a mechanism wherein the iridium center and pendent carboxylate jointly mediate the concerted removal of a proton and an electron from a C–H bond through excited-state oxidative PCET, generating the reduced and protonated complex IrII−1H.

Computational modeling of reaction thermochemistry with cyclohexane also supports a concerted mechanism of abstraction (Figure 6B). Alkyl radical formation from C–H bonds via sequential proton transfer followed by electron transfer (PT/ET) mediated by *IrIII−1 is prohibitively endergonic given the high C–H pKa of cyclohexane (∆GPT = +81.5 kcal mol−1). Similarly, an ET/PT pathway beginning with initial oxidation of cyclohexane to cyclohexyl radical cation is highly unfavorable (∆GET = +42.8 kcal mol−1). A concerted mechanism of abstraction, however, is predicted to be favorable (∆GPCET = −6.0 kcal mol−1).

An alternative mechanism for the observed quenching behavior is direct hydrogen-atom transfer from a carboxyl radical generated by intramolecular oxidation of the pendent carboxylate base.55 However, oxidation of the pendent carboxylate would generate a reduced ground state IrII complex, IrII−1•, which is a weak H-atom acceptor (BDFEO–H = 43 kcal mol−1) and thus is not competent to mediate C–H abstraction. Furthermore, the LMCT event leading to the formation of IrII−1• would not exhibit a concentration dependence on the alkane substrate, as is observed experimentally. Based on our observations of linear concentration-dependent quenching, abstraction from ground-state carboxyl radical IrII−1• is unlikely and is thus occurring from an excited-state species, although the electronic structure of this excited state is unclear. Taken together, these results suggest that the predominant mechanism for C–-H bond homolysis is via concerted PCET with an excited state of IrIII−1.

### Development of Catalytic C–H Alkylation Reaction

We next sought to investigate a catalytic C–H functionalization platform leveraging both the excited-state properties of the deprotonated IrIII state and the reducing nature of the resultant protonated IrII complex. We envisioned that irradiation of the Ir-carboxylate photocatalyst IrIII−1 with visible light generates the excited-state *IrIII−1 (Figure 7). This species engages an alkyl substrate through oxidative C–H PCET, generating the reduced and protonated form of the catalyst IrII−1H and an alkyl radical. Addition of the nascent radical into an appropriate electron-deficient olefin partner forms the corresponding electron-withdrawing group stabilized alkyl radical. Subsequent stepwise ET/PT or concerted reductive PCET from IrII−1H regenerates IrIII−1 and furnishes the C–H alkylated product in a net redox-neutral fashion wherein the Ir complex acts as both H-atom acceptor and H-atom donor.

Cyclohexane 1 (BDFEC–H = 91 kcal mol−1)56 was selected as a test substrate for reaction evaluation and optimization (Table 1). Following irradiation of a solution containing two equivalents of 1, 2 mol% IrIII−1 and one equivalent of benzylidene malononitrile 2b in acetonitrile for 18 hours under 456 nm irradiation at 35 °C, we observed trace yield of alkylated product 1b (entry 1). Optimization efforts identified chlorobenzene as an optimal solvent (see SI for details), producing 1b with 79% yield (entry 2). Increasing alkane loading to three equivalents provided 1b in increased yield of 86% (entry 3). Further reducing the alkane loading to 1 equivalent furnished 1b at comparable yield of 62% (entry 4). Dimethyl fumarate 2a proved to be a similarly favorable acceptor for the cyclohexyl radical, generating 1a in 67% yield (entry 5). The omission of the photocatalyst or light resulted in no product formation (entries 6–7). Analogous complex [Ir(dF(CF3)ppy)2(4,4’-dCO2Me-bpy)]PF6 ([IrIII−1Me]PF6), which possesses a similar oxidation potential to IrIII−1 but does not contain a Brønsted basic moiety, failed to generate product (entry 8).

### Mechanistic Investigations

#### Excited-state dynamics of *IrIII−1 and *IrIII−2

To gain deeper insight into the electronic structure of the abstracting species and its excited-state dynamics, we employed TAS and quantum mechanical modeling (Figure 8). We first used ultrafast TAS to characterize the excited-state dynamics of the deprotonated catalysts IrIII−1 and IrIII−2.57 Experiments revealed that the initial excited-state of IrIII−1 resembles a triplet MLCT state localized on a phenylpyridine (3MLCTppy). This state likely forms after excitation of a ground-state singlet to a π* orbital via 1MLCTppy, which then undergoes rapid intersystem crossing (ISC) to 3MLCTppy on a faster timescale than the resolution of our experiment.58

Analysis of the dynamics in the picosecond regime are then well described by three transient lifetimes: τ1(*IrIII−1) = 1.9 ps, τ2(*IrIII−1) = 123 ps, and an unresolved long-lived lifetime (Figure 9A, Figure S35). The evolution-associated difference spectrum (EADS) for τ1(*IrIII−1) shows growing signals at 390 and 500 nm, as well as a broad decay of central features around 410 and 450 nm (see SI). We assign this first lifetime to intramolecular vibrational relaxation, consistent with previous reports on similar iridium complexes.59-61 The major lifetime in this regime, τ2(*IrIII−1), is primarily associated with depletion of the central excited state absorption features from 400 to 500 nm (Figure 9B). Ligand-to-ligand charge transfer (LLCT) has been detected in heteroleptic Ir complexes with similar spectral signatures and is often observed on the low-picosecond timescale. Therefore, we tentatively assign τ2(*IrIII−1) to a LLCT from the 3MLCTppy to the bipyridine ligand.62-66

The unresolved lifetime component was then investigated with nanosecond resolution experiments. The long-lived dynamics of *IrIII−1 are well described by a biexponential model with lifetimes τ3(*IrIII−1) = 260 ns and τ4(*IrIII−1) = 1.3 μs, with most decay accounted for by τ3(*IrIII−1). Therefore, we assign τ3(IrIII−1) as recombination of electrons in the lowest-lying triplet state (3MLCTbpy) to the ground state. Notably, the lifetimes of this complex suggest that the excited state of the complex is sufficiently long-lived to engage in diffusion-controlled bimolecular chemistry. Likewise, the steady-state emission spectra of IrIII−1 and [IrIII−1H]PF6 suggest a bipyridine-localized MLCT due to protonation-dependent emission behavior and observed photobasicity (vide supra). The excess electronic density contributed to the bipyridine upon excitation to the 3MLCTbpy state inductively increases the basicity of the proximal carboxylate, in line with our observations.

To further study the excited state of the *IrIII−1 complex, we visualized the natural transition orbitals (NTOs)67 of the lowest-lying excited triplet state of IrIII−1 with TDDFT using the methods described above. The computed NTOs further support our spectral assignments, as seen in the increased electronic population of the bipyridine ligand in the lowest-lying excited triplet state (Figure 9C). Attempts to optimize the geometry of higher-lying triplet states converged to the same geometry with the same energy and character of the lowest-lying excited triplet state (see SI S14.2), signifying that the 3MLCTbpy triplet state is the lowest-energy excited state.

Analogous spectroscopic and computational investigations were performed to understand the dynamics of *IrIII−2, with an emphasis on understanding the influence of peripheral ligand modulation (cf. *IrIII−1). The dynamics in the picosecond regime are fitted with three transient lifetimes, denoted τ1(*IrIII−2), τ2(*IrIII−2), and an unresolved long-lived component (Figure 10A). Initially, we observe a decay of features between 410 and 460 nm, as well as a broad increase in signal centered around 500 nm, with a lifetime of τ1(*IrIII−2) = 0.48 ps. Additionally, a π-π* transition below 475 nm grows with τ1(*IrIII−2), which is not fully resolved in the probed wavelength range due to scattering of light from the pump pulse (Figure 10B). This spectral shift indicates vibrational relaxation among triplet MLCT states. However, as the excited-state absorption (ESA) features of the *IrIII−2 lifetimes are more localized than in *IrIII−1, the dynamics of τ1(*IrIII−2) are likely dominated by 3MLCTppy states. With τ2(*IrIII−2) = 23 ps, there is further depletion of ESA between 410 and 450 nm, as well as a subtle rise around 480-510 nm (see Figure S36 and section S15). We therefore assign this population shift to equilibration and LLCT between low-lying triplet states, as reported in similarly ligated IrIII complexes.68-70

To resolve the long-lived component, we again measured the dynamics in the nanosecond regime. The recombination dynamics of *IrIII−2 are adequately fit with a single exponential lifetime of τ3 = 2 μs. We hypothesize that the significant extension of the relaxation lifetime in *IrIII−2, compared to the major component in *IrIII−1, may be due to thermal equilibration between 3MLCTppy and 3MLCTbpy populations. To investigate the possible involvement of multiple triplet excited states in the dynamics of *IrIII−2, we computationally characterized the excited triplet states of *IrIII−2 and *IrIII−2H. Interestingly, although *IrIII−2H is characterized by a single, low-lying 3MLCTbpy state, its deprotonated analogue revealed two energetically proximal triplet states, with the lowest-energy triplet state (T1) characterized as a 3MLCTppy state (Figure 10C). The second, slightly higher-lying (+5.0 kcal mol−1) triplet state (T2) of *IrIII−2 is characterized as a 3MLCTbpy state. The extended lifetime and unique protonation-state dependent lowest-lying excited states are the focus of ongoing studies on the reactivity of *IrIII−2 (vide infra).

### Mechanism of C–H Bond Formation

Having focused on the initial abstraction, we next considered the mechanism of C–H bond formation in our alkylation protocol. An analogous ferrocene-anilinium photo-electrocatalyst reported by Peters possessed an N–H BDFE of 37 kcal mol−1 and was competent in the reduction of olefins via a PCET mechanism. This led us to consider that the proposed post-abstraction species, IrII−1H, could serve as a potent reductant and possible H atom source with a weak O–H bond (BDFEO–H = 43 kcal mol−1), either via a stepwise ET/PT pathway or concerted H-atom donation to form C–H bonds (Figure 11). Computational analysis of optimized structures shows that concerted bond formation in the reduction of the cyclohexane methyl acrylate adduct I is expected to be −34.7 kcal mol−1 exergonic to furnish product III. By contrast, the stepwise pathways are computed to be +6.5 kcal mol−1 endergonic for initial ET to generate II, followed by a thermodynamically favorable PT (−41.2 kcal mol−1) to deliver product III. While these results indicate that reductive PCET is a viable pathway for the formation of the resultant product C–H bond, additional experimental efforts will be required to further investigate this hypothesis.

### Scope of C–H Alkylation

With a more thorough understanding of the ability of IrIII−1 and IrIII−2 to both abstract and form C–H bonds, we sought to explore the scope of accessible substrates, with an emphasis on regioselectivity and C–H bond strength. Through our scope studies, we showed the scope of the reaction with olefins 2a and 2b for each substrate (Figure 12). A variety of C(sp3)–H substrates and C(sp2)–H substrates proved amenable to the alkylation protocol. Unactivated hydrocarbons such as cyclohexane and cyclooctane underwent alkylation in good yields (2–3). Adamantane produced secondary and tertiary alkylation products in 1:1 r.r. (4a, 4b), notably with less regioselectivity compared to other HAT catalysts (decatungstate 5:1 r.r.; TBHP ~7:1 r.r.).72,73 Cyclohexanone underwent alkylation to produce a mixture of β- and γ-regioisomers in >10:1 r.r. (5a, 5b), with no alkylation at the acidic α-carbonyl site. Activated α-heteroatom substrates, such as cyclic ethers (6–7), azetidine and pyrrolidine substrates proved to be efficient reaction partners (8–10), providing exclusive selectivity for hydridic α-heteroatom positions. We also observed alkylation of the activated primary C–H bond of methyl tert-butyl ether (11) and acetanilide (12) with good yields.

Alkylation of N,N-dimethyl formamide resulted in the formation of a mixture of formyl and methyl abstraction products in 1.1:1 r.r. (13b). Similarly, N,N-dimethylacetamide provided product in good yield (14a, 14b). Reaction of the C(sp2)–H bonds of benzaldehyde and p-anisaldehyde with dimethyl fumarate 1a resulted in yields of 58% and 71% (15a, 16a), respectively, while reaction with benzylidene malononitrile 1b resulted in significantly diminished yields of 20% and 23% (15b, 16b). Interestingly, alkylation of benzylic C–H bonds occurred readily with benzylidene malononitrile as a radical acceptor. The functionalization of 4-methylanisole occurred at both the benzylic and α-oxygen sites in 4.5:1 r.r., producing the alkylated product in combined 68% yield (17b). Ethylbenzene also underwent alkylation to yield a 10:1 mixture of regioisomers at the secondary and primary sites in good yield (18b).

Given the high BDFE of IrIII−1, we were curious whether these complexes could abstract atypically strong C–H bonds. To this end, cubanes possess exceptionally strong C–H bonds (BDFEC–H = 105 kcal mol−1) due to their strained nature and increased s-character. As a result, direct C(sp3)–H functionalization of cubanes remains challenging.74,75 Gratifyingly, when 1,4-cubane dimethyl ester was subjected to the standard reaction conditions, the alkylated product 19a was obtained in a 16% yield, which was unambiguously characterized by single crystal X-ray diffraction (Figure 12).

In contrast to our previous C–H PCET platform, which was intolerant of substrates containing protic E–H bonds, substrates containing free O–H and N–H bonds were well tolerated and provided C–H alkylation products (20b, 21a, 21b). We posited that while O–H and N–H PCET processes may occur simultaneously and reversibly, only C–H PCET followed by radical addition to the olefin led to the formation of product. Interestingly, the catalyst could mediate olefin hydrosilylation, though this process could also include established chain mechanisms following initial Si–H abstraction (22a).76

Using this C–H alkylation method, we validated the spectroscopically determined KIE by steady-state emission with IrIII−1 by performing an intermolecular competition experiment in which one equivalent of dimethyl fumarate was exposed to 5 equivalents each of cyclohexane and deuterated cyclohexane. We observed a product distribution corresponding to a KIE of 1.3, comparable to the isotope effects observed in the luminescence quenching experiments described above (Figure 13A).

To compare the reactivity of the two complexes, we also evaluated IrIII−2 as a catalyst in the C–H alkylation transformation. The excited-state catalyst *IrIII−2 proved to be an effective abstractor of hydridic C–H bonds and exhibited different selectivity compared to *IrIII−1. We observed that *IrIII−2 performed better when irradiated with 427 nm light. For example, 4-methylanisole underwent alkylation at both the benzylic and α-oxygen positions with diminished regioselectivity but improved yield relative to IrIII−1 (2:1 r.r. and 91% yield vs 4.5:1 r.r. and 68% yield). Furthermore, despite being modestly endergonic based on thermochemical analysis, IrIII−2 was also able to mediate the abstraction of the strong C–H bonds in 1,4-cubane dimethyl ester yielding 19a in 14% yield (Figure 13B). The origins of this change in reactivity are unclear and suggest that the excited-state electronic structure, as influenced by peripheral ligands, has significant effects on PCET reactivity and bond selectivity. We hypothesize that the comparable reactivity of *IrIII−2, despite contradicting thermochemical data, could potentially be a result of its extended excited-state lifetime and/or the involvement of higher-lying excited states.

## Conclusion

In summary, we developed iridium polypyridyl complexes IrIII−1 and IrIII−2 with pendent Brønsted basic carboxylates whose excited states exhibited high BDFEs and long lifetimes. These Ir complexes proved to be effective excited-state abstractors for C–H bonds with BDFEs up to 105 kcal mol−1 and mediated the alkylation of unactivated C–H substates. Mechanistic, computational, and spectroscopic studies suggest that the photocatalyst mediated both C–H abstraction and C–H bond formation via PCET mechanisms from a bpy-based triplet MLCT excited state. We are optimistic that these constructs will create new opportunities to generalize oxidative PCET towards C–H functionalization. Further efforts to understand ligand structure-activity relationships within this family of complexes and their subsequent synthetic applications are ongoing.
